title: What Does MCP Consulting Look Like in 2026?
description: MCP consulting in 2026 — what to expect, what to pay, and how to pick a Claude implementation partner without overpaying the Big Four.
author: Sophie Cave
content:
A year ago, “MCP consulting” was not a category. Today it is a market. Anthropic has put real money behind a partner network, the Big Four are staffing dedicated Claude practices, and a wave of boutique shops have launched with one job: help companies wire up the Model Context Protocol without setting their data on fire.

If you are evaluating a partner — or thinking about becoming one — this is the field guide. We run an MCP practice ourselves at Like One, ship production servers every week, and watch the competitive landscape closely. Here is what MCP consulting actually looks like in 2026, what it costs, and how to tell the real practitioners from the rebranded SEO agencies.

What MCP Consulting Actually Is

MCP consulting is the practice of helping an organization integrate the Model Context Protocol into its workflows. That sounds narrow. In practice the work splits across five distinct competencies.

Server engineering is the obvious one — building MCP servers that expose internal systems to AI agents. A custom CRM connector, a database query layer, a deployment tool, a domain-specific reasoning module. This is where most engagements start.

Workflow design is the part most agencies skip. A server is useless if the workflow around it is wrong. Good consultants spend at least as much time on what tools to expose, in what order, with what guardrails, as they do on the code itself. The difference between a working agent and a dangerous one is usually a workflow decision, not a code decision.

Security review is non-optional. Every MCP server you install gets the same permissions as the agent calling it. A compromised server can exfiltrate data, run arbitrary commands, or manipulate the agent through prompt injection. Real consultants audit before they integrate.

Agent architecture is the bigger picture — how Claude, the MCP servers, your existing systems, and your humans interact. Which decisions stay with the human? Which run autonomously? Which trigger an approval workflow? This is where the engagement either delivers measurable productivity or becomes shelfware.

Change management is the part nobody puts on their pitch deck. Your team has to use this thing. If the new agent breaks the way three departments work, it does not matter how elegant the server design is. The consultants who deliver durable wins are the ones who plan for adoption from day one.

The State of the Market

In March 2026 Anthropic announced a $100 million investment in the Claude Partner Network. The launch members are exactly who you would expect: Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, KPMG, Cognizant, Infosys, Slalom, Tribe AI, and Turing. Entry is gated by the Claude Certified Architect exam, which means the partner stamp at least implies someone in the building has passed a real technical test.

That investment matters because it sets the going rate. When the Big Four staff a practice, they bill it at Big Four rates. Boutique shops anchor to that ceiling and undercut it. Solo practitioners undercut the boutiques. The pricing tiers below all exist because Anthropic put $100M behind enterprise consulting.

The market signals beyond Anthropic's investment are louder than most people realize. SAP and Anthropic announced a deep partnership at SAP Sapphire 2026, bringing Claude into the world's largest ERP install base. Guidepoint launched an MCP server exposing more than 100,000 expert transcripts to AI agents. Abacor shipped an MCP connector for CPA and accounting workflows. Every major vertical software vendor is now staring at the same question: do we ship our own MCP server, or do we wait for our customers to demand one?

The answer they are landing on is the same answer enterprises landed on for APIs in 2015 and SDKs in 2010: ship it before the competition does, and hire someone who has done it before to get it right.

Who Is Hiring MCP Consultants

Three buyer profiles dominate the current market.

Mid-market SaaS companies hire MCP consultants to ship a Claude integration alongside their existing product. The pitch is straightforward — your customers are using Claude, they want Claude to talk to your software, and shipping an MCP server is faster than building a full agent layer yourself. Engagements typically run six to twelve weeks and end with a published server plus internal documentation.

An MCP server also doubles as marketing in 2026. Showing up in the MCP registry is increasingly how new buyers discover infrastructure tools. The companies hiring for this work treat it like SEO investment a decade ago — a few months of engineering that pays back in distribution for years.

Enterprise IT teams hire MCP consultants to wire up internal Claude deployments. They have data that cannot leave the network, workflows that cannot tolerate hallucination, and compliance requirements that rule out most off-the-shelf agents. This is where the Big Four win deals — the procurement process favors firms that can produce a SOC 2 report and a six-figure invoice.

Founders and operators hire MCP consultants to build internal AI systems. A custom memory layer, a deployment automation, a research assistant trained on the company's own documents. These are the most interesting engagements because they often produce something the company could not have specified in advance. Good consultants in this segment work iteratively — ship something small, see what the founder actually uses, double down on that.

What MCP Consulting Costs in 2026

Pricing splits cleanly into four tiers.

Big Four and global SI: $300–$600 per hour, or $250K–$2M for a full engagement. You are buying procurement compliance, audit-friendly documentation, and a name your CIO can defend on a slide. The work itself is often subcontracted to the same boutique engineers you could have hired directly for a third of the cost.

Specialist boutiques: $200–$400 per hour, or $50K–$250K per engagement. Firms like claudeimplementation.com and fastslowmotion.com live in this tier. You get senior engineers who have shipped MCP servers before, faster cycle times than the Big Four, and a smaller team that actually understands your codebase.

Solo specialists and small teams: $150–$300 per hour, or $5K–$50K per project. This is where most production MCP work happens in 2026. The trade-off is bandwidth — a solo specialist can ship faster than a boutique on a single project but cannot run five concurrent engagements. Our own consulting tier sits here, starting from $500 per month for ongoing retainer work.

Generalist freelancers: $50–$150 per hour. This tier exists, but be careful. The MCP ecosystem is new enough that most freelancers learned the protocol in the last few months. They can ship a basic server, but they will not catch the security issues that matter and they will not push back when you ask for the wrong architecture.

The right tier depends on what you are buying. If you need procurement-friendly enterprise delivery, the Big Four are unavoidable. If you need a working MCP server in your codebase in three weeks, hire a boutique or a solo specialist. If you need cheap, hire a freelancer and budget for the inevitable rework.

Big Four vs Boutique vs Solo: The Honest Comparison

The pitch decks all promise the same outcome. The reality is different at each tier.

The Big Four deliver process. You get weekly status decks, a named partner, a methodology document, and a deliverable that survives a procurement audit. What you do not always get is the senior engineer the proposal promised. The standard pattern is one partner, one manager, and four offshore developers — most of whom learned MCP last quarter. The work ships, but the cost-to-value ratio is rough unless you specifically need the audit trail.

Boutiques deliver craft. The senior engineer in the pitch is the senior engineer who writes the code. Engagement scope is tighter, cycles are faster, and the work usually reflects current best practices rather than 2024-era patterns. The risk is bandwidth — boutiques often run multiple engagements concurrently, so your project can stall if their bigger client has a fire.

Solo specialists deliver speed. One brain, one codebase, no internal handoffs. You can ship an MCP server end-to-end in a week if the scope is right. The risk is bus factor — if the consultant gets sick, the project pauses. Mitigate by demanding source code in your repo from day one and complete handoff documentation as part of the deliverable.

We are obviously biased — Like One is a solo-specialist operation. But the bias is informed. We have watched Big Four engagements wrap up with a working server that nobody on the client team can maintain, because the actual builders left when the contract ended. We have watched boutique engagements stall for months when the lead engineer got pulled onto a bigger client. And we have watched solo specialists ship complete, documented, production-ready systems in the time it takes a Big Four team to schedule the kickoff call.

How to Evaluate an MCP Consultant

Most evaluation criteria for software consultants apply here. A few are MCP-specific.

  1. Ask to see a server they have shipped. Not a screenshot. Not a case study. A GitHub link or a registry entry. If they cannot produce one, they have not shipped MCP work before. Move on.
  2. Ask how they handle security. A good answer mentions credential isolation, input validation, prompt injection defenses, dependency auditing, and minimal permission scope. A bad answer is “we follow best practices.”
  3. Ask about their stack opinions. Do they prefer Python or TypeScript for server work? When do they use each? What is their position on hosted vs local servers? Real practitioners have strong, specific opinions. Generalists have none.
  4. Ask what they would NOT build. A consultant who will build anything you ask for is a consultant who will build the wrong thing. The best practitioners push back on bad ideas before they take your money.
  5. Ask about post-engagement support. MCP servers need maintenance — model updates, dependency patches, evolving security best practices. What is the handoff plan? Who maintains the server after the engagement ends?

Red Flags

The consulting market always attracts opportunists. The MCP gold rush is no different. Watch for these patterns.

The pivoted generalist agency — a web development or marketing agency that added “MCP consulting” to its services page in the last quarter. They will ship something. It will not be good. If their case studies are mostly WordPress sites and their lead engineer cannot name three MCP servers from memory, they are not who you want.

The certification-heavy proposal — a proposal that leads with badges, partnerships, and certifications instead of shipped work. The Claude Partner Network membership is meaningful but it is not a substitute for a portfolio. Ask what they actually built before the certification arrived.

The blank-check proposal — a proposal with vague scope, time-and-materials billing, and no clear deliverable. This is how engagements drift from $40K to $400K. Demand fixed scope or fixed budget. Real practitioners can estimate MCP work because they have shipped it before.

The vendor-neutral pitch — a consultant who claims expertise across Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, and every open source agent framework. The depth is not there. MCP is Anthropic’s protocol; the consultants who matter for MCP work specialize in Claude. Cross-platform breadth is a different service.

The Claude Partner Network in 2026

Anthropic's partner network is the biggest formal credentialing system in the space. Membership requires the Claude Certified Architect exam ($99, five domains, 720/1000 to pass). Once in, partners get co-marketing, lead routing, and early access to new APIs.

For buyers, partner membership is a signal but not a guarantee. The launch members are global SIs with hundreds of engineers, most of whom have never touched MCP. The certification establishes a floor of technical knowledge, not a ceiling. Treat it the way you treat AWS Solutions Architect certification — useful filter, not sufficient evidence.

For practitioners, partner membership is becoming table stakes. The CCA exam is cheap. Passing it removes a friction point for enterprise procurement and unlocks the registry of leads Anthropic routes to partners. If you take MCP consulting seriously as a business, you take the exam.

What We Actually Do

For full transparency — here is how our own MCP consulting practice operates. We ship custom MCP servers, audit existing ones for security, and design Claude Code workflows that replace specific manual processes. Engagements typically run two to six weeks from kickoff to deployed server.

Our credentials are five published open source MCP servers (security auditing, accessibility testing, code signing, design systems, visual inspection), thirty-six technical blog posts on Claude and MCP, and a production system that runs our own operations — nine hundred-plus brain entries, seventy-four hundred-plus semantic vectors, a Telegram-fronted agent gateway. The Like One Foundation is a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit, which means a portion of every consulting dollar funds HIV cure research at UCSF.

That is the model. Specialist depth, production proof, transparent pricing, and a giving structure baked into the business. Pricing starts at $500 per month for ongoing retainer work and scales with scope. See our consulting page for current packages.

Where MCP Consulting Goes Next

Three shifts are already visible.

Vertical specialization will dominate the next twelve months. Healthcare MCP, legal MCP, accounting MCP, financial services MCP. Abacor's CPA connector and Guidepoint's expert-network server are the early examples. Generalist consultants will compete on price; specialists will compete on outcomes. Specialists win the better engagements.

Productization will pull margin out of pure services. Boutiques that ship a reusable MCP server alongside engagements will see better economics than firms that bill purely for hours. The same dynamic killed pure-play web design agencies a decade ago. Expect the same pressure on pure-play MCP consultancies.

Open source signals will matter more than badges. The buyers who know what they are doing will look at GitHub history before they look at certifications. Published servers, active issues, real downloads. The MCP registry has become the new portfolio. Consultants without a registry presence will increasingly look like SEO agencies without a sample site — plausible until you ask the obvious question.

If you are considering MCP consulting for your organization, the buying decision is simpler than it looks. Define the outcome you need, find a practitioner who has shipped that outcome before, and ignore the badges. If you are considering MCP consulting as a practice, the business is real — but only if you ship public work that proves you can do the job. The badges will follow.

Most companies hire to skip the learning curve, not the work.
